documentation.content:
# Dry Bean

This dataset explores morphological differences among seven dry bean varieties and presents a **multiclass-classification** problem in which individual bean samples are classified from numerical shape measurements extracted from images.

The objective is not only to obtain a predicted class, but also to understand how morphological measurements separate the observed varieties and how effectively a multiclass model generalizes to previously unseen samples.

The analysis is predictive rather than causal. Relationships between morphology and bean class describe patterns within the observed data and should not be interpreted as causal or agronomic effects.

## Dataset overview

Each row represents a single dry bean grain described by numerical morphological measurements extracted from images.

| Item | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| Bean samples | 13,611 |
| Source columns | 17 |
| Predictive features | 16 |
| Target | `Class` |
| Target classes | 7 |
| Problem type | Multiclass classification |
| Source | UCI Machine Learning Repository |
| UCI dataset ID | `602` |

The target column is never used as a predictive feature.

The seven target classes are:

- `BARBUNYA`
- `BOMBAY`
- `CALI`
- `DERMASON`
- `HOROZ`
- `SEKER`
- `SIRA`

The predictive features describe different aspects of bean geometry, including overall size, perimeter, principal-axis dimensions, elongation, convexity, roundness, compactness, and derived shape factors.

The model starts from numerical measurements that have already been extracted from bean images. It does not reproduce the original image acquisition, segmentation, or feature-extraction process.

## Analytical question

The analysis investigates two related questions:

1. **How do the observed morphological characteristics differ among the seven bean varieties?**
2. **How effectively can those measurements be used to classify previously unseen bean samples?**

Because the input variables describe physical morphology, substantial differences between classes are expected. However, observed relationships do not establish that an individual measurement determines bean variety independently of the remaining feature profile.

The classification task therefore focuses on the combined predictive information contained in the 16 numerical measurements.

## Data quality and preparation

The source contains 13,611 observations and 16 numerical candidate features.

The preparation process preserves the source observations without generic imputation, row removal, or automatic outlier deletion. All 16 validated predictive features remain available to the model.

The evaluated workflow uses a stratified train-validation-test split with random seed `42`:

| Partition | Approximate share | Purpose |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Train | 70% | Model fitting |
| Validation | 15% | Model evaluation and development decisions |
| Final test | 15% | Final holdout evaluation |

The evaluated partitions contain 2,040 validation observations and 2,044 final-test observations.

The final-test partition is kept outside model fitting and is evaluated only during finalization.

Repeated feature profiles can occur in the source. Because the dataset does not provide an observation identifier, exact equality between two feature vectors is not sufficient evidence that the corresponding records represent the same physical grain.

This distinction is important when reasoning about potential duplicates or leakage: repeated measurements alone do not establish duplicate identity.

## Class distribution

The seven classes are not equally represented.

`DERMASON` is the most frequent class, while `BOMBAY` is the least frequent.

| Class | Rows | Share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| SEKER | 2,027 | 14.89% |
| BARBUNYA | 1,322 | 9.71% |
| BOMBAY | 522 | 3.84% |
| CALI | 1,630 | 11.98% |
| DERMASON | 3,546 | 26.05% |
| HOROZ | 1,928 | 14.17% |
| SIRA | 2,636 | 19.37% |

The majority-to-minority support ratio is approximately `6.79`.

![Dry Bean target class distribution](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/target_class_distribution.png)

Because class support is unequal, predictive performance should not be evaluated using accuracy alone.

Macro-averaged metrics are especially useful because they give each class equal influence on the aggregate result regardless of class frequency.

## Key exploratory findings

### Morphological measurements contain strong class information

Several size and shape measurements show substantial univariate association with bean class.

The strongest exploratory associations include:

- `Area`;
- `ConvexArea`;
- `EquivDiameter`;
- `Perimeter`;
- `MinorAxisLength`;
- `MajorAxisLength`.

![Univariate feature-to-target associations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/feature_target_association_ranking.png)

These results show that bean morphology contains substantial information about class identity.

They do not imply that individual features should be interpreted independently or causally. Classification depends on the joint information contained across the morphological profile.

### The feature space contains substantial structural redundancy

Several morphological measurements are strongly related.

Examples include:

- `Area` and `ConvexArea`;
- `Area` and `EquivDiameter`;
- `Perimeter` and `EquivDiameter`;
- `AspectRatio` and `Eccentricity`;
- `Compactness` and `ShapeFactor3`.

The exploratory analysis identifies 21 feature pairs meeting the predefined redundancy-review threshold.

![Numerical feature correlation heatmap](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/numerical_feature_correlation_heatmap.png)

Strong correlation does not automatically imply that one of the related features should be removed.

Correlated variables can still contribute useful predictive information to nonlinear models, and feature removal should be supported by model-evaluation evidence rather than correlation alone.

The complete validated feature set is therefore retained.

### Some bean classes have overlapping morphological profiles

The seven classes do not occupy completely isolated regions of the feature space.

Exploratory class-profile analysis identifies:

- `DERMASON` and `SIRA` as the closest pair by robust central-profile distance;
- `BARBUNYA` and `CALI` as the pair with the greatest mean central IQR overlap.

![Standardized Dry Bean class profiles](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/standardized_class_profiles.png)

A two-component PCA projection captures approximately 81.9% of the standardized exploratory variance and provides another view of class structure and overlap.

![Exploratory PCA projection](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/class_pca_projection.png)

The projection shows that substantial class structure exists even in a compressed two-dimensional representation, while some varieties remain partially overlapping.

PCA position and profile overlap are descriptive evidence only. They do not directly estimate classifier error.

## Model selection evidence

The model comparison considers four machine-learning families under a stratified multiclass evaluation design:

- Logistic Regression;
- Decision Tree;
- Random Forest;
- HistGradientBoosting.

HistGradientBoosting with all 16 predictive features produces the strongest validation result under the predefined selection policy.

![Validation model comparison](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/model_validation_comparison.png)

Feature-policy sensitivity is also evaluated rather than assuming that correlated or derived variables should automatically be removed.

Removing `ShapeFactor2` produces only a small decrease in validation Macro F1, while removing the broader set of confirmed derived features produces a substantially larger reduction.

![Feature policy sensitivity](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/feature_policy_sensitivity.png)

This evidence supports retaining all 16 features in the final predictive configuration.

The selected model uses:

```text
model family         = hist_gradient_boosting
learning_rate        = 0.05
max_iter             = 250
max_leaf_nodes       = 15
min_samples_leaf     = 40
l2_regularization    = 0.0
class_weight         = None
random_seed          = 42
```

The resulting model is a `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` trained to distinguish all seven classes simultaneously.

## Model evaluation

The final holdout evaluation contains 2,044 previously unseen test observations.

| Metric | Final test |
| --- | ---: |
| **F1 Macro** | **0.9433** |
| Balanced Accuracy | **0.9436** |
| Recall Macro | 0.9436 |
| F1 Weighted | 0.9340 |
| Accuracy | 0.9340 |
| Log Loss ↓ | 0.1942 |

Performance is strong across all seven classes.

| Class | Recall |
| --- | ---: |
| BARBUNYA | 0.9347 |
| BOMBAY | 1.0000 |
| CALI | 0.9510 |
| DERMASON | 0.9323 |
| HOROZ | 0.9516 |
| SEKER | 0.9441 |
| SIRA | 0.8914 |

`SIRA` is the most difficult class in the final holdout evaluation, with recall of approximately 89.1%.

The residual classification errors are not distributed uniformly across all classes. They are concentrated more strongly around varieties with morphologically similar or overlapping feature profiles.

This is consistent with the exploratory evidence showing overlap between classes such as `DERMASON` and `SIRA` and between `BARBUNYA` and `CALI`.

The reported results describe performance under the defined random-snapshot evaluation protocol. They do not establish temporal, external, or production generalization.

## Understanding the evaluation metrics

### F1 Macro — 0.9433

Macro F1 calculates an F1 score independently for each class and then gives every class equal weight in the final average.

This is particularly appropriate for Dry Bean because the seven classes have unequal support.

A large class such as `DERMASON` therefore does not dominate the final score merely because it contains substantially more observations than a smaller class such as `BOMBAY`.

**Higher values are better.**

Macro F1 is the primary evaluation metric for this classification workflow.

### Balanced Accuracy — 0.9436

Balanced Accuracy averages recall across the seven classes.

It helps reveal whether predictive performance remains broadly distributed across classes rather than being driven mainly by the most frequent categories.

**Higher values are better.**

Although its numerical value is slightly higher than Macro F1, the two metrics answer somewhat different questions. Balanced Accuracy focuses directly on recall, while Macro F1 incorporates both precision and recall for each class.

### Accuracy — 0.9340

Accuracy represents the proportion of test observations assigned to the correct bean class.

It provides an intuitive overall measure of classification success, but each individual observation contributes equally. Classes with more observations therefore exert more influence on the result than smaller classes.

For this reason, Accuracy is best interpreted alongside Macro F1 and Balanced Accuracy rather than as the sole measure of model quality.

**Higher values are better.**

The numerical values of different metrics should not be interpreted as directly competing quantities. Each summarizes a different aspect of multiclass classification performance.

### Log Loss — 0.1942

Log Loss evaluates the full probability distribution produced by the classifier rather than only the final predicted class.

It penalizes confident probability assignments when the corresponding prediction is wrong, making it useful as a complement to label-based metrics.

**Lower values are better.**

## Multiclass prediction and result interpretation

Prediction requires the same 16 numerical morphological measurements used during model development.

These measurements span four broad aspects of bean morphology:

- size and dimensions;
- proportions and elongation;
- compactness and convexity;
- derived shape factors.

For each observation, the classifier produces a probability distribution across all seven target classes.

There is no positive class because this is a multiclass rather than a binary-classification problem.

The decision strategy is:

`argmax`

The class receiving the highest model probability is returned as the predicted class.

For example, if the model assigns:

```text
BARBUNYA   0.03
BOMBAY     0.01
CALI       0.86
DERMASON   0.02
HOROZ      0.04
SEKER      0.01
SIRA       0.03
```

the predicted class is:

```text
CALI
```

because it has the highest probability.

No binary classification threshold is involved in this decision.

The class probability distribution can provide useful information about ambiguity. A highly concentrated distribution indicates that the model strongly favors one class, while similar probabilities across multiple classes indicate greater uncertainty between morphologically overlapping alternatives.

These probabilities should still be interpreted as outputs of the fitted classifier within the observed feature space, not as guarantees about the biological identity of an arbitrary future specimen.

## What this dataset demonstrates

Dry Bean provides a technically rich example of tabular multiclass classification using numerical measurements derived from images.

It demonstrates several important aspects of applied predictive modeling:

- exploratory analysis of multiclass structure;
- unequal class support;
- deterministic data preparation;
- stratified train, validation, and test partitions;
- comparison of multiple classifier families;
- evaluation of feature-retention policies;
- nonlinear classification using HistGradientBoosting;
- macro-averaged performance metrics;
- per-class evaluation;
- multiclass probability outputs;
- residual confusion between morphologically similar classes.

The dataset also illustrates why multiclass performance cannot be understood from overall accuracy alone.

Macro F1 and Balanced Accuracy provide complementary class-aware views of performance, while per-class recall reveals where residual errors remain concentrated.

Finally, the class-probability distribution preserves more information than the final `argmax` prediction alone and can expose cases in which multiple varieties receive similar model support.

## Limitations

Several important boundaries remain:

- the evaluation is based on a random stratified snapshot rather than a temporal, prospective, or external validation dataset;
- the model receives image-derived numerical features rather than raw bean images;
- the original image-acquisition, segmentation, and feature-extraction processes are outside the evaluated predictive workflow;
- exploratory feature associations do not establish causal or agronomic relationships;
- morphological overlap remains between some classes;
- evaluation on this dataset does not establish equivalent performance for beans collected under different imaging equipment, environments, cultivars, or populations;
- exact equality between feature profiles cannot establish duplicate physical grains because the source provides no observation identifier;
- class probabilities have not been established as universally calibrated measures of biological certainty;
- no deployment-time distribution-shift evaluation is demonstrated;
- no production monitoring or dataset-drift policy is evaluated;
- the analysis does not establish operational, industrial, or commercial suitability.

## Responsible interpretation

The evidence supports a clear predictive conclusion:

> In this dataset, numerical measurements of bean size and shape contain strong information for distinguishing seven dry bean varieties. A HistGradientBoosting multiclass model using all 16 morphological features achieves a final-test Macro F1 of approximately 0.9433 and Balanced Accuracy of approximately 0.9436. Performance remains strong across all seven classes, although morphological overlap and residual confusion remain for some varieties.

These results demonstrate effective classification within the observed dataset and evaluation protocol.

They should not be interpreted as evidence that any individual morphological measurement causally determines variety, nor as proof that the model will maintain the same performance on beans collected under different acquisition conditions or populations.

Use of the model beyond this analytical setting would require independent validation of the complete measurement pipeline, representative external data, probability behavior, distribution stability, and application-specific error costs.
